passage: Near the village school's water tank, four children were playing stapu on squares scratched into the mud. Dolma, five, stood at the edge holding her flat stone. "Can I play?" Anirban, drawing the last square, didn't look up. "No. You can't play with us. You're too small." Dolma didn't cry. She stood very still, stone in her fist, then sat on the steps, bent over. When the cook-didi rang the lunch bell, Dolma said, "My tummy hurts." Didi sat beside her and held her close. After a while she walked Dolma back and asked Anirban to show her how to throw.

qa.q: What were the four children playing near the water tank?
qa.a: They were playing stapu on squares scratched into the mud.

qa.q: What does Dolma's "My tummy hurts" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests being left out hurt her like a real pain in her body, even though she didn't cry.

qa.q: What did the cook-didi do that helped?
qa.a: Didi sat close and held her, then asked Anirban to show Dolma how to throw, which gave Dolma a way back into the game.

qa.q: What might Anirban learn from being asked to teach Dolma the throw?
qa.a: Anirban might see that "too small" only means she needs showing, and notice how much the words hurt her.

grounding: A young child told she cannot play freezes and says her tummy hurts, showing exclusion felt as physical pain.

passage: In the park behind the nursery in Leeds, Freya and two other girls had squeezed into the wooden playhouse. Mina, five, ran over in yellow wellies. "Can I be the baby?" "No," said Freya, holding the door shut. "You can't play with us. It's full." Mina's face crumpled. She cried, then went quiet and pressed both hands on her stomach. When her mum came, Mina whispered, "My tummy hurts." Her mum knelt in the wet grass and asked what happened. Mina pointed at the playhouse. Her mum hugged her. "That hurt your feelings, and feelings can hurt in your tummy too." Then they fed the ducks together.

qa.q: What did Mina ask to be in the game?
qa.a: Mina asked, "Can I be the baby?"

qa.q: Why might Mina press both hands on her stomach after crying?
qa.a: Being shut out hurt so much that it felt like a real ache in her tummy.

qa.q: What did Mina's mum choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: She knelt, asked what happened, hugged Mina and named the hurt, so Mina felt believed and comforted.

qa.q: How might Freya see the playhouse moment?
qa.a: Freya may think she was only keeping the house from getting too full, without noticing how much her words hurt Mina.

grounding: A young child shut out of a game cries, goes quiet and says her tummy hurts, and her mother recognises the hurt as real.

passage: At the anganwadi, after the midday khichdi, the children built a train from plastic chairs. Wasim was the engine. Suraj, five, dragged over a chair. "I'm the last carriage." "No," said Wasim. "You can't play with us. You pushed yesterday." The chairs shuffled closer. Suraj froze, lips pressed tight. Later he told Kamla-tai his stomach was paining. She felt his forehead, then took him on her lap. "Did the train say no?" He nodded into her sari. Kamla-tai called Wasim over. "Suraj, can you say sorry for yesterday's push? And every train needs a guard." She gave Suraj her whistle.

qa.q: What did the children build after the midday khichdi?
qa.a: They built a train out of plastic chairs.

qa.q: What does Suraj freezing with lips pressed tight suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt shocked and hurt at being shut out, holding the pain in instead of crying.

qa.q: Which of Kamla-tai's choices helped Suraj back into the game?
qa.a: She took his stomach-ache seriously, guessed the real hurt, asked for a sorry about the push, and gave him a guard's role with a whistle.

qa.q: Why might Wasim have said no, and how might Wasim feel when Kamla-tai steps in?
qa.a: Wasim may still be upset about yesterday's push; hearing a sorry and staying the engine may make it easier to let Suraj join.

grounding: A young child told he cannot play freezes and complains of a stomach ache, and a caregiver treats the exclusion as a real hurt.

passage: I'm Parul. I was on the bench by our building's sandpit when this happened to my little cousin Kiran. He is four. Three bigger children were making a castle. Kiran ran over with his spade. "Can I help?" A girl in a pink cap said, "No. You can't play with us. You'll break it." Kiran stood very still, holding his spade. Then he walked back slowly and climbed onto the bench. "My tummy is hurting," he said, face in my arm. I held him. "That felt bad, didn't it?" He nodded. Later we dug our own tunnel.

qa.q: What was Kiran holding when he was told he couldn't play?
qa.a: He was holding his spade.

qa.q: What does Kiran saying his tummy hurts suggest?
qa.a: It suggests being left out made him feel a real, body-felt hurt, even though he could not name it as sad.

qa.q: What did Parul do that helped Kiran?
qa.a: Parul held him, named the feeling for him and then played with him, so he felt comforted and not alone.

qa.q: Why might the girl in the pink cap have said no to Kiran?
qa.a: She may have been worried that a small child would break the castle, without noticing how much her words would hurt him.

grounding: A four-year-old told he can't play freezes and says his tummy hurts, showing exclusion felt as physical pain, as seen by his cousin.

passage:
Monday. At playschool, Minakshi, five, asked to play house. Vishal shook his head. "You can't play with us. We already have a mummy." Minakshi froze. At snack time she said her tummy hurt and left her banana.

Wednesday. Minakshi stood near the house corner, holding her stomach. The teacher sat with her. "Being left out hurts, doesn't it?" Minakshi nodded, eyes wet.

Friday. The teacher said, "Every house needs a neighbour who brings sweets." Vishal thought, then said, "You can be the neighbour." Minakshi carried plastic laddoos over. She ate her whole banana.

qa.q: What did Vishal say when Minakshi asked to play house on Monday?
qa.a: He said, 'You can't play with us. We already have a mummy.'

qa.q: What does Minakshi holding her stomach on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the hurt of being left out felt like a real pain in her body.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped by Friday?
qa.a: The teacher named Minakshi's hurt and then suggested a new role, the neighbour, so Vishal could include her without giving up his game.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel when he lets Minakshi join as the neighbour?
qa.a: Vishal might feel pleased to keep his game while adding a friend, finding that including her made the play better.

grounding: A five-year-old told she can't play freezes and says her tummy hurts, showing that exclusion feels like physical pain, until a teacher helps her join.
